name: Yonggom
sweep_summary: Yonggom (yong1280) is not in the catalog. The sweep's single title hit (Glottolog 155352, 'How snake lost its feet') is an SIL-PNG vernacular storybook that matched on 'feet'; it is not about stress (priority none). Beyond the sweep list, the Glottolog 5.1 dump gives three descriptive works by Steve Christensen: the 2002 SIL Organised Phonology Data (SIL URL dead, sil.org/pnglanguages Cloudflare-403, no Wayback capture), the 2000/2013 reference grammar (SIL archive 55514, 'Not Available Online'), and the 2010 discourse paper in Pacific Linguistics 616, which is open (ANU repository) and already on file; it states first-hand, p. 1: 'Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word, and the language uses intonation rather than being a tonal language.' Zahrer's 2023 Muyu dissertation (on file) carries Christensen 2013:4-5 with examples showing initial primary stress plus trochaic secondary stresses, and notes Drabbe 1954 reports final accent for the Ninati/Metomka dialects and that Kawip Muyu has no lexical stress. Acquisition priority: high for Christensen 2013 grammar and 2002 OPD (both SIL Ukarumpa only).

new_statements.quote: Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word, and the language uses intonation rather than being a tonal language.
new_statements.citation: Christensen, Steve. 2010. Yongkom discourse: ergativity and topic. In Joan Hooley (ed.), Papers on six languages of Papua New Guinea, 1-39. Pacific Linguistics 616. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU.
new_statements.reading: Fixed initial (word-initial) primary stress, no lexical tone, for the Kabom/Kagaip dialect of Yongkom spoken along the Ok Tedi (author's own 1991-2004 SIL fieldwork). Corroborated by the carried report of Christensen's 2013 reference grammar (Zahrer 2023:51-52): initial stress realised by loudness and pitch, with trochaic secondary stresses in longer words. A fixed-initial coding for a new yong1280 record would rest on this open, first-hand sentence; the 2013 grammar or the 2002 OPD would be the stronger source if either becomes reachable.

sources.quote: The language has contrastive vowel length, which is represented orthographically by writing the vowel twice. [...] Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word, and the language uses intonation rather than being a tonal language.
sources.note: First-hand (author lived with the Yongkom 1991-2004 under SIL; data = Kabom/Kagaip dialect of the Ok Tedi villages): fixed initial primary stress; no lexical tone. One sentence in a discourse paper; no examples, no statement about secondary stress or exceptions.

sources.quote: Zahrer 2023:51-52: 'Christensen reports the lexical stress (realised as "both increase in loudness and pitch" (p. 4)) always to be on the first syllable. Although he does not explicitly mention secondary stress, his example words comprise symbols for primary and secondary stress: (70) Christensen's (2013:5) lexical stress in Yonggom: ["ka.bak] axe, ["u.ni.,tap] bent, ["ki.a.,mu.nE] like-that, ["bi.aN.,ga.nE.,wEn] you removed, ["ka.na.,wa.na.,wan.di.,wEn] they surrounded. ... Christensen analyses Yonggom words to have metrical stress with a disyllabic foot and trochaic meter.'
sources.locator: Christensen 2013 pp. 4-5 as reported by Zahrer 2023, sect. 2.4.1, pp. 51-52
sources.note: The fullest statement for this language: initial primary stress (loudness + pitch), with alternating secondary stresses on odd syllables in the examples (trochaic, left-to-right). Consistent with Christensen 2010. Only reachable as a carried quote; the SIL manuscript itself is not online and no library copy was found in the audit.
